facts.label: Leverage and coverage
facts.text: Year-end leverage was high and stable before the sales: gross debt was 3.55x, 3.29x and 3.37x reported EBITDA at the end of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and net debt was 3.10x at the end of 2025. In the third quarter of 2026 the sale proceeds repaid the revolver, both term loans and the 4.75% notes due 2027, leaving the 8.25% notes due 2029 and the Kansas mortgage note, which is why gross debt is now 1.45x adjusted earnings. The mechanism that matters to creditors is that the claim is smaller and longer-dated but backed by fewer owned facilities: property and equipment fell from USD 2,132.2 million to USD 1,822.8 million while CoreCivic continues to run the sold facilities under existing federal contracts. The consequence is better leverage and cover with weaker asset backing and a concentration on one federal customer, and the supplied documents do not commit the remaining proceeds to debt reduction rather than buybacks. Basis: calculation K05; calculation K07; calculation K29; 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 162; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 2

facts.text: Cash conversion was weak even before the sales. Fiscal 2025 operating cash flow was USD 194.6 million against reported EBITDA of USD 362.1 million because receivables and other assets absorbed USD 145.0 million. facts.label: Liquidity and maturities
facts.text: Liquidity at 30 September 2026 was USD 547.2 million of cash plus USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver after USD 23.5 million of letters of credit. Scheduled principal is small until 2029: USD 1.6 million for the rest of 2026, USD 6.9 million in 2027 and USD 7.4 million in 2028, then USD 508.0 million in 2029 when the 8.25% notes fall due. The credit agreement allows unlimited restricted payments only while its secured leverage ratio is at or below 1.50x and the notes indenture only while its total leverage ratio is at or below 2.00x. Adjusted gross debt of 1.45x earnings is below both levels but is not either covenant measure, and covenant headroom cannot be calculated because the covenant definitions were not supplied. facts.label: Data quality and definition risks
facts.text: Five definition points limit how the figures can be used. The issuer reports net leverage of negative 0.1x at 30 September 2026 without a definition, while carrying-value debt exceeds cash on the balance sheet; the figure is consistent with leaving out the Kansas notes, which sit in an unrestricted subsidiary, but the issuer does not say so. Reported EBITDA is the primary denominator under the method, but the sale gain makes the trailing figure meaningless, so adjusted ratios are shown beside it and are labelled as built from a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 figure. The earlier source readiness note called USD 629.6 million total debt; that is principal, and the carrying value used here is USD 623.1 million. Gross interest is printed only to one decimal in millions for the full years, so fiscal EBITDA is exact to about USD 0.05 million. Segments changed in the second quarter of 2026 and fiscal 2025 has not been recast. limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- High: the issuer's net leverage of negative 0.1x at 30 September 2026 has no stated definition and cannot be reproduced from carrying-value debt and cash, which restricts any use of the issuer's ratio for the latest date; the action that would close it is the issuer's net debt definition or the third quarter supplemental financial information. - High: no document states trailing twelve-month or full-year adjusted EBITDA, so the fiscal 2023, 2024 and 2025 adjusted figures and the trailing adjusted figure are house-built from the issuer's own add-back categories; the action is the fourth quarter 2025 results release. - Medium: reported EBITDA for the trailing twelve months to 30 September 2026 includes the sale gain, so the reported leverage and cover ratios for that date are not meaningful; the action is to read the adjusted ratios. - Medium: segments were redefined in the second quarter of 2026 and fiscal 2025 on the new basis is not printed, which restricts any segment trend across 2025 and 2026; the action is a recast fiscal 2025 segment schedule. - Medium: the covenant definitions are not supplied, only the covenant levels (a total leverage ratio of not more than 4.50 to 1.00, a secured leverage ratio of not more than 2.50 to 1.00 and a fixed charge coverage ratio of not less than 1.75 to 1.00), so covenant headroom is not calculable; the action is the executed credit agreement. - Low: undrawn revolver availability at 31 December 2023 is not printed in the supplied documents, so the liquidity chart has no 2023 undrawn figure. - Low: gross interest expense for the full years is printed only in millions to one decimal, so fiscal EBITDA and the cover ratios carry a rounding uncertainty of about USD 0.05 million; the action is the issuer's full-year reconciliation. - Low: the Kansas notes are non-recourse secured notes of an unrestricted subsidiary and no source states their legal rank against the Bank Credit Facility or the 8.25% notes, so they are left out of the debt stack. - Low: carrying values by instrument are not printed; unamortized issuance costs are printed to one decimal for each note, so one financing cost adjustment row is used in the instrument register. - Low: balance sheets at 31 March, 30 June and 30 September 2025 are not supplied, so no 2025 quarter-end net debt is shown and the issuer's net leverage of 2.5x at 30 September 2025 cannot be checked. - Low: source dashes in the statement tables (no impairments in some periods, no debt repayment expenses in some periods, no contingent consideration before 2026, no acquisitions in 2023 and 2024) are shown as not supplied rather than as zero. - Low: the nine-month 2025 segment revenue is printed with a total that differs from consolidated revenue by the small other revenue line, which the segment table does not itemise; the segment revenue rows are not summed to consolidated revenue.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Federal demand is the credit: federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue, up from 51% in 2024, and ICE alone was 35%, so occupancy, contract renewal and appropriations at one customer family drive cash flow. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against concern is the balance sheet: carrying-value debt fell below cash plus undrawn revolver, the only maturity of size is the 8.25% notes due in 2029, and ICE demand is strong, with occupancy up and a new five-year contract awarded in August 2026. The view would improve if the revised contracts for the sold facilities keep current economics, if two of them renew before August 2027, and if sale proceeds keep going to debt reduction rather than repurchases. It would worsen if ICE terminated or re-priced contracts at the sold facilities, if further repurchases or acquisitions were funded with new debt, or if federal appropriations or detention priorities shifted. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, CoreCivic presents an adequate business profile supported by long federal relationships, high occupancy and a pharmacy and services line that diversifies revenue, but credit quality is constrained by concentration in one federal customer family and by capital returns that can absorb the cushion created by the facility sales. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: earnings are rising on activations, while free cash flow conversion is thin. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the 8.25% notes due April 2029 and on how much of the USD 1,098.7 million of liquidity is returned to shareholders. The primary downside path is a fall in federal detention demand or a re-pricing of the sold facilities' contracts. Further analysis would require the executed credit agreement and indenture, the proxy statement, and the revised contract terms. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: federal customer concentration. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M01

facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The downside is issuer-specific. The initiating condition is a repeat of early 2026, when nationwide ICE detention fell by about 10,500 individuals from a January high of about 70,800, or a contract change at the four sold facilities after the change of ownership. The first operational break is occupancy: the Residential segment margin was 22.3% in the third quarter of 2026 against 22.5% a year earlier even in a strong quarter, and margin for nine months fell to 22.8% from 24.0% when populations dipped. Because costs are largely fixed, lower occupancy cuts EBITDA faster than revenue and free cash flow, already thin, turns negative. Liquidity of about USD 1,098.7 million absorbs a long period of weak cash flow, and leverage would rise from 1.45x trailing adjusted EBITDA, with the 4.50x covenant maximum far above that level although its definition was not supplied, so resilience appears sufficient to avoid a liquidity problem before 2029 unless repurchases use the cushion. Management levers are idle-facility activation timing, capex deferral and repurchase restraint. The observable triggers are ICE population, occupancy and any change to the sold facilities' contracts. ## Findings
### Bottom line

The ten supplied CoreCivic documents are sufficient to build the requested credit snapshot from primary filings, but headline leverage, trailing earnings and segment trends need explicit handling before creditors rely on them.

The latest balance sheet is dated 30 September 2026, after the July and August facility sales and the repayment of the revolver, both term loans and the 2027 notes, so year-end 2025 figures describe a materially different capital structure. The third quarter release reports a negative net leverage multiple although printed debt exceeds printed cash, no trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA is printed, and segments were redefined in the second quarter of 2026. No executed credit agreement, indenture, rating, market quote or peer data was supplied, so covenant headroom, ratings, relative value and recovery work stay conditional.

## Findings
### Bottom line

CoreCivic's net debt fell from USD 1,122.8 million at the end of 2025 to USD 75.9 million at 30 September 2026 after four facility sales, so leverage is now low, but the fall rests on one-off proceeds and earnings are still rebuilding.
Basis: calculation K26; calculation K27; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 14

On trailing adjusted earnings of USD 429.8 million, built from the 2025 annual statements and the 2026 releases, gross debt is 1.45x and cash interest is covered 5.10x. Reported EBITDA includes the USD 1,770.7 million sale gain, so ratios on it are not meaningful. Operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 266.6 million for the nine months because USD 518.7 million of tax on the gains was paid in cash.

Basis: calculation K28; calculation K29; calculation K30; calculation K31; calculation K32; calculation K33; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4
### Leverage and coverage

Year-end leverage was high and stable before the sales: gross debt was 3.55x, 3.29x and 3.37x reported EBITDA at the end of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and net debt was 3.10x at the end of 2025. In the third quarter of 2026 the sale proceeds repaid the revolver, both term loans and the 4.75% notes due 2027, leaving the 8.25% notes due 2029 and the Kansas mortgage note, which is why gross debt is now 1.45x adjusted earnings. The mechanism that matters to creditors is that the claim is smaller and longer-dated but backed by fewer owned facilities: property and equipment fell from USD 2,132.2 million to USD 1,822.8 million while CoreCivic continues to run the sold facilities under existing federal contracts. The consequence is better leverage and cover with weaker asset backing and a concentration on one federal customer, and the supplied documents do not commit the remaining proceeds to debt reduction rather than buybacks.
Basis: calculation K05; calculation K07; calculation K29; 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 162; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 2
### Cash flow quality

Cash conversion was weak even before the sales. Fiscal 2025 operating cash flow was USD 194.6 million against reported EBITDA of USD 362.1 million because receivables and other assets absorbed USD 145.0 million. For the nine months to September 2026 operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 266.6 million because USD 518.7 million of income tax was paid, primarily on the gain on the sale of the four facilities, while the proceeds arrived in investing cash flow as USD 2,113.4 million of net proceeds from asset sales. Financing outflows of USD 1,166.3 million included USD 561.1 million of share repurchases, so the cash balance rose to USD 547.2 million from USD 97.9 million, and the next move in net debt depends on further buybacks against future operating cash flow.
Basis: calculation K21; 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 163; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 67
### Liquidity and maturities

Liquidity at 30 September 2026 was USD 547.2 million of cash plus USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver after USD 23.5 million of letters of credit. Scheduled principal is small until 2029: USD 1.6 million for the rest of 2026, USD 6.9 million in 2027 and USD 7.4 million in 2028, then USD 508.0 million in 2029 when the 8.25% notes fall due. The credit agreement allows unlimited restricted payments only while its secured leverage ratio is at or below 1.50x and the notes indenture only while its total leverage ratio is at or below 2.00x. Adjusted gross debt of 1.45x earnings is below both levels but is not either covenant measure, and covenant headroom cannot be calculated because the covenant definitions were not supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 66; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 16
### Data quality and definition risks

Five definition points limit how the figures can be used. The issuer reports net leverage of negative 0.1x at 30 September 2026 without a definition, while carrying-value debt exceeds cash on the balance sheet; the figure is consistent with leaving out the Kansas notes, which sit in an unrestricted subsidiary, but the issuer does not say so. Reported EBITDA is the primary denominator under the method, but the sale gain makes the trailing figure meaningless, so adjusted ratios are shown beside it and are labelled as built from a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 figure. The earlier source readiness note called USD 629.6 million total debt; that is principal, and the carrying value used here is USD 623.1 million. Gross interest is printed only to one decimal in millions for the full years, so fiscal EBITDA is exact to about USD 0.05 million. Segments changed in the second quarter of 2026 and fiscal 2025 has not been recast.

- High: the issuer's net leverage of negative 0.1x at 30 September 2026 has no stated definition and cannot be reproduced from carrying-value debt and cash, which restricts any use of the issuer's ratio for the latest date; the action that would close it is the issuer's net debt definition or the third quarter supplemental financial information.

- High: no document states trailing twelve-month or full-year adjusted EBITDA, so the fiscal 2023, 2024 and 2025 adjusted figures and the trailing adjusted figure are house-built from the issuer's own add-back categories; the action is the fourth quarter 2025 results release.

- Medium: reported EBITDA for the trailing twelve months to 30 September 2026 includes the sale gain, so the reported leverage and cover ratios for that date are not meaningful; the action is to read the adjusted ratios.

- Medium: segments were redefined in the second quarter of 2026 and fiscal 2025 on the new basis is not printed, which restricts any segment trend across 2025 and 2026; the action is a recast fiscal 2025 segment schedule.

- Medium: the covenant definitions are not supplied, only the covenant levels (a total leverage ratio of not more than 4.50 to 1.00, a secured leverage ratio of not more than 2.50 to 1.00 and a fixed charge coverage ratio of not less than 1.75 to 1.00), so covenant headroom is not calculable; the action is the executed credit agreement.

- Low: gross interest expense for the full years is printed only in millions to one decimal, so fiscal EBITDA and the cover ratios carry a rounding uncertainty of about USD 0.05 million; the action is the issuer's full-year reconciliation.

- Low: the Kansas notes are non-recourse secured notes of an unrestricted subsidiary and no source states their legal rank against the Bank Credit Facility or the 8.25% notes, so they are left out of the debt stack.
- Low: carrying values by instrument are not printed; unamortized issuance costs are printed to one decimal for each note, so one financing cost adjustment row is used in the instrument register.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Creditors are now lending to a government contractor that has sold four owned facilities to its largest customer and repaid most of its debt, so credit quality rests on federal contract renewals and on how shareholder returns are balanced against that cushion.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 10; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3

Federal agencies produced 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE alone 35%, and ICE can end any contract for convenience or lack of appropriation. The four sold facilities remain under contracts that the company expects to modify, and two of them expire in August 2027. A new chief executive took over on 24 September 2026, and the board has twice raised the repurchase authorization, by USD 500.0 million each time.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 74
### Key findings

- Federal demand is the credit: federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue, up from 51% in 2024, and ICE alone was 35%, so occupancy, contract renewal and appropriations at one customer family drive cash flow. Every ICE contract can be ended for convenience or non-appropriation, which turns a strong 2026 into a revenue stream that depends on continued political demand rather than on contract protection.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54

- Selling the four facilities to the federal government turned owned collateral into cash but left CoreCivic operating the sites for the buyer: gross proceeds were about USD 2.2 billion, USD 716.3 million of debt was repaid, and two of the four management contracts expire in August 2027. Lower debt improves solvency, while weaker asset backing and a customer that now owns the real estate reduce bargaining power at renewal.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation B02; calculation B03

- Capital allocation has moved from debt repayment to shareholder returns within weeks: a USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase was paid on 10 August 2026, and the board added USD 500.0 million to the authorization on 4 August and again on 3 November, for a total of USD 1,700.0 million. Whether creditors keep the post-sale cushion depends on covenant limits that the supplied documents describe but do not define.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 75; calculation B04

- Operating momentum is real: occupancy was 84.0% in the third quarter of 2026 against 76.7% a year earlier, four idle facilities were activated since early 2025, and a new five-year contract for the Appleton facility is expected to add about USD 75.0 million of annual revenue when fully activated. This supports earnings but the activation costs and the idle capacity still held are a drag until demand fills them.
Basis: EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 11

- Governance is adequate for monitoring but incomplete for control: audited statements, an internal control opinion and quarterly reconciliations are available, the chief executive changed on 24 September 2026 after health-related resignation, and ownership concentration, board composition and related-party dealings are not established because the proxy statement was not supplied. The sponsor and governance risk level is Medium.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 153; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 154
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against concern is the balance sheet: carrying-value debt fell below cash plus undrawn revolver, the only maturity of size is the 8.25% notes due in 2029, and ICE demand is strong, with occupancy up and a new five-year contract awarded in August 2026. The view would improve if the revised contracts for the sold facilities keep current economics, if two of them renew before August 2027, and if sale proceeds keep going to debt reduction rather than repurchases. It would worsen if ICE terminated or re-priced contracts at the sold facilities, if further repurchases or acquisitions were funded with new debt, or if federal appropriations or detention priorities shifted.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7
### Limitations

- The 2026 proxy statement was not supplied, so ownership concentration, board composition and related-party dealings are not established, which keeps the governance risk level at Medium rather than allowing a firmer view.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 154

- The terms of the revised management contracts for the four sold facilities are not disclosed, so margin and revenue on those facilities after the change in ownership are not established, which limits the confidence of the view on asset backing.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54

- The executed credit agreement and notes indenture were not supplied, so whether buybacks and further asset sales are inside covenant capacity is not established, which limits how far the creditor-alignment reading of capital allocation can be pushed.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
- Fiscal 2025 is not recast to the new segments, so statements about segment mix rest on the third quarter of 2026 and on the earlier basis for fiscal 2025 separately.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 202

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Four detention facilities were sold to the United States through the Department of Homeland Security in two pairs: California City and Otay Mesa on 2 July 2026 and Appleton and Midwest on 4 August 2026, for gross proceeds of about USD 2.2 billion and a gain of USD 1,770.7 million. CoreCivic continues to manage them under ICE contracts expected to be modified, and the company says its discussions with ICE about buying further facilities are preliminary.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation B03

The proceeds repaid USD 716.3 million of debt: the revolver, the Incremental Term Loan, the Initial Term Loan and the 4.75% senior notes due 2027, which were redeemed at a make-whole price on 12 August 2026. The only debt left is the 8.25% senior notes due 2029 and the Kansas mortgage note; the only new term debt in 2026 was the USD 100.0 million Incremental Term Loan of 10 April 2026.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation B02

A USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase agreement was paid on 10 August 2026, with final settlement expected before the end of the second quarter of 2027, and CoreCivic acquired Clinical Solutions Pharmacy on 1 April 2026 for an estimated USD 199.6 million including an earn-out.
Basis: EX99.1_2026-06-30_cxw_d118761dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 75

## Findings
### Bottom line

CoreCivic's credit profile has strengthened sharply on the balance sheet after the 2026 facility sales, but it remains a single-customer business whose cash flow depends on federal detention demand, so the profile is adequate rather than strong.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 54

Net debt fell to USD 75.9 million at 30 September 2026 from USD 1,122.8 million at the end of 2025, liquidity is about USD 1,098.7 million, and the only sizeable maturity is USD 500.0 million of 8.25% notes due in 2029. The primary downside is a federal shift in detention priorities or re-pricing of the sold facilities' contracts, made worse if repurchases use the cash cushion.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M01; calculation M02; calculation M03; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 52
### Key findings

- The balance sheet is repaired, but by one-off proceeds: gross debt at carrying value fell to USD 623.1 million and net debt to USD 75.9 million at 30 September 2026, against USD 1,122.8 million of net debt at the end of 2025, because four facilities were sold for about USD 2.2 billion. Lower debt cuts interest and refinancing risk, while the repair cannot be repeated without selling more owned assets.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M02; calculation M03

- Leverage and cover are now comfortable on adjusted earnings: gross debt is 1.45x trailing adjusted EBITDA of USD 429.8 million and that earnings figure covers cash interest 5.10x, against 3.37x reported leverage and 5.03x cover at the end of 2025. The adjusted figure is built partly from a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 number, and the issuer's own net leverage claim below zero cannot be reproduced, so the ratios are estimates rather than settled facts.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M04; calculation M05

- Cash conversion is the weakest part of the financial profile: free cash flow was USD 54.0 million in fiscal 2025 on adjusted EBITDA of USD 365.6 million and an outflow of USD 397.7 million over the last twelve months because USD 518.7 million of tax on the sale gains was paid. Thin conversion means debt service depends on EBITDA rather than on retained cash flow, so lower occupancy would reach liquidity quickly.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M06

- Customer concentration is the dominant business risk: federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE alone 35%, and every ICE contract can be ended for convenience or non-appropriation. Revenue visibility is therefore political rather than contractual, and the federal buyer of the four facilities now also owns the assets behind the management contracts.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M07

- Liquidity and the maturity wall are favourable: cash of USD 547.2 million and USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver are about USD 1,098.7 million, while scheduled principal is below USD 10.0 million a year until USD 508.0 million falls due in 2029. This makes a refinancing squeeze unlikely before 2029 unless the cushion is spent.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M01

- Capital allocation is the main creditor-adverse risk: a USD 500.0 million accelerated repurchase was paid in August 2026, the authorization was raised by USD 500.0 million twice and USD 755.8 million remained available after the November increase. Repurchases compete with repaying the 2029 notes, and the executed covenant documents that limit them were not supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M08
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against concern is the combination of near-zero net debt, large liquidity and rising federal demand: nationwide ICE detention populations rebounded from an April 2026 trough to a higher level by July 2026, the issuer's occupancy rose to 84.0% against 76.7% a year earlier, and management cites funding for ICE secured through September 2029. The view would improve if the revised contracts for the sold facilities kept current economics, if the 2029 notes were refinanced or repaid early, and if repurchases were held to operating cash flow. It would worsen if ICE populations fell again as in early 2026, if the sold facilities' contracts were re-priced or ended, or if buybacks or acquisitions were funded with new debt.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 52; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Limitations

- Trailing earnings rest partly on a house-adjusted fiscal 2025 figure because no full-year adjusted EBITDA is printed, so the leverage and cover ratios could differ by the add-backs the issuer would choose and the view of comfortable leverage is an estimate.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1)
- The issuer's own net leverage figure below zero has no stated definition and is not used, so the claim that net leverage is near zero rests on carrying-value debt and cash built here.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1)
- Covenant levels are printed but not their definitions, so the judgement that leverage and liquidity are comfortable is not tested against the tests that bind or against restricted payment capacity.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
- The revised management contract terms for the sold facilities are not disclosed, so the revenue durability judgement assumes current economics continue.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A)
- No agency rating, market price or peer set was supplied, so the profile is an absolute assessment and says nothing about relative value against other issuers.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
### Overall credit view

Overall, CoreCivic presents an adequate business profile supported by long federal relationships, high occupancy and a pharmacy and services line that diversifies revenue, but credit quality is constrained by concentration in one federal customer family and by capital returns that can absorb the cushion created by the facility sales. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: earnings are rising on activations, while free cash flow conversion is thin. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the 8.25% notes due April 2029 and on how much of the USD 1,098.7 million of liquidity is returned to shareholders. The primary downside path is a fall in federal detention demand or a re-pricing of the sold facilities' contracts. Further analysis would require the executed credit agreement and indenture, the proxy statement, and the revised contract terms. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: federal customer concentration.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M01
### Downside scenario

The downside is issuer-specific. The initiating condition is a repeat of early 2026, when nationwide ICE detention fell by about 10,500 individuals from a January high of about 70,800, or a contract change at the four sold facilities after the change of ownership. The first operational break is occupancy: the Residential segment margin was 22.3% in the third quarter of 2026 against 22.5% a year earlier even in a strong quarter, and margin for nine months fell to 22.8% from 24.0% when populations dipped. Because costs are largely fixed, lower occupancy cuts EBITDA faster than revenue and free cash flow, already thin, turns negative. Liquidity of about USD 1,098.7 million absorbs a long period of weak cash flow, and leverage would rise from 1.45x trailing adjusted EBITDA, with the 4.50x covenant maximum far above that level although its definition was not supplied, so resilience appears sufficient to avoid a liquidity problem before 2029 unless repurchases use the cushion. Management levers are idle-facility activation timing, capex deferral and repurchase restraint. The observable triggers are ICE population, occupancy and any change to the sold facilities' contracts.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-Q_2026-09-30_cxw.htm.jsonl, page 16; calculation M01; calculation M04
### Strengths and weaknesses

- Strength: balance sheet repair. Net debt of USD 75.9 million against USD 1,122.8 million at the end of 2025 follows the sale of four facilities and repayment of USD 716.3 million of debt; this reduces interest and removes the 2027 maturity, so default risk before 2029 is low unless the cash is distributed.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M02; calculation M03

- Strength: liquidity. Cash of USD 547.2 million and USD 551.5 million undrawn on the revolver give about USD 1,098.7 million against scheduled principal below USD 10.0 million a year until 2029, so a squeeze is unlikely.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M01
- Strength: demand and occupancy. Occupancy of 84.0% and the new Appleton contract expected to add about USD 75.0 million of annual revenue support earnings as idle capacity is activated.
Basis: EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX99.1_2026-09-30_cxw_d165428dex991-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7

- Weakness: customer concentration. Federal agencies were 54% of 2025 revenue and ICE terminates for convenience, so a policy change reaches revenue directly and the buyer of the sold assets is the same counterparty.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M07

- Weakness: thin cash conversion. Free cash flow was USD 54.0 million in fiscal 2025 and an outflow of USD 397.7 million for the last twelve months, so debt service relies on EBITDA and liquidity rather than retained cash.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M06

- Weakness: shareholder-friendly capital allocation. USD 500.0 million repurchased in August and USD 755.8 million of authorization left after the November increase can consume the cushion, and the limits were not supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation M08
